results.summary: This project implements a hardware-optimized Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog, designed for area efficiency while maintaining biological realism. It accepts two 3-bit channel inputs and provides a 7-bit membrane voltage output plus a spike output. Configuration parameters are loaded serially via a load mode and serial data pin. The design is intended for educational or research use in spiking neural networks, and requires only simple external hardware such as switches, LEDs, or a 7-segment display for interaction.

This Morse Code Trainer is an interactive learning game that displays letters on a 7-segment display and challenges users to input the correct Morse code pattern using a switch. It provides immediate feedback and progresses through the English alphabet. The design can be tested in simulation or on hardware. It requires a 7-segment display and a switch for user input.

This tile is an experimental silicon art tile that plays with the idea of crossing traditional crafts like weaving with the weaving-like work of entangled transistor lines. It has no functional purpose and is meant to be appreciated visually after decapping the chip. No testing is required or possible. The artwork will be unveiled when decapping the chip.

This project implements a simple SAR ADC controller designed to work with external analog circuitry. It outputs an 8-bit DAC control signal and accepts a comparator input to perform successive approximation. The design requires an external R-2R ladder network and a comparator to function. It has no end-of-conversion signal, and the start input must be toggled to initiate conversions.

This project implements an Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire (AdExp) neuron in Verilog, consisting of a neuron core and a parameter loader. It supports loading parameters via a nibble interface and provides a spike output and debug values. The design is self-contained and requires no external components. Testing involves loading parameters to induce spiking and observing the spike output within a set time limit.

This project explores a delta-sigma ADC implemented digitally using flip-flops as quantizers and switched-capacitor lines for reference and measurement. It outputs pulse-density modulated signals and filtered 13-bit values, with a difference output representing the ADC code. The design requires external capacitors, resistors, and a current source/sink for operation. It aims to evaluate PVT effects and mismatch on ADC linearity, with an effective resolution of 11 bits.

This project is a simple RISC-V processor supporting the RV32E base instruction set plus Zicond and Zbs extensions. It uses two independent SPI memory interfaces for instruction and data storage, and provides 8 GPIO inputs and 8 GPIO outputs. The processor begins execution from address 0x0 and requires external SPI ROM and RAM for operation. A test program is provided that records GPIO inputs and outputs them after a delay to verify functionality.
